title: The roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8–9)
hook: be sober and watch: read every Tuesday at night prayer
tomorrow: a thousand years as a day

segments.voice: Yesterday, the worry thrown like a cloak onto a colt. Your line was he hath care of you. How many times did you toss it back? Day six hundred eleven.

It's late on a Tuesday. In a monastery chapel, a convent, a hospital break room, a bedroom with a phone propped on the pillow, people are praying the last prayer of the Church's day, called Compline, or Night Prayer. The lights are low. The psalm is done. And the short reading for Tuesday night is two verses from the end of First Peter. For centuries, in the older form of the prayer, those same verses opened Compline every single night. Of all the lines in scripture, the Church chose these to say right before the lights go out.
screen: `LATE ON A TUESDAY.` → `NIGHT PRAYER: COMPLINE.` → `TWO VERSES BEFORE LIGHTS OUT.`

segments.voice: Here they are in the Douay-Rheims: "Be sober and watch: because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about seeking whom he may devour." Two commands first. Be sober: the Greek means clear-headed, not drunk, not foggy. And watch: stay awake, keep alert. That second word has a history for Peter. On the night before Jesus died, in the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus asked Peter to watch with him for one hour. Peter fell asleep. Three times. Now here is the same man, years later, telling the whole Church: stay awake. He knows exactly what it costs not to. Then the picture: a lion, prowling, roaring, looking for someone to swallow. Lions hunt at night, and they look for the one that's drifted from the herd. That's why the verse belongs at bedtime. The Church teaches that the devil is real, a fallen creature, but a creature: not God's equal, with limits on what he can do. So Peter doesn't say run, or panic. He says, "Whom resist ye, strong in faith." Stand your ground. And he adds something easy to miss: your brothers and sisters all over the world are going through the same sufferings. The lion picks off the one who's alone. The answer is a clear head, open eyes, and a whole flock. Night Prayer was built for exactly this. It begins with a short look back over the day, and it ends by entrusting the night to God.
screen: `BE SOBER: CLEAR-HEADED.` · `WATCH: PETER SLEPT IN THE GARDEN.` · `THE LION LOOKS FOR THE ONE ALONE.` · `RESIST, STRONG IN FAITH.` · then, large: `BE SOBER AND WATCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end the day watchfully. Wherever you are, sit up a little, as if you were keeping watch. Breathe. Then walk back through today, slowly, from now to this morning. Where were you clear-headed? Where did you drift, scroll, or snap? Don't judge it. Just see it, the way a watchman sees the walls. Notice one moment you'd like to handle differently tomorrow. If you pray, you can hand the night to God, or pray a line from Compline if you know one. If you don't, just close the day with your eyes open to it. The bell holds the time.
The roaring lion. First Peter five: the adversary prowls, so stay clear-headed and awake, and stand firm together. Today's word.
Your line: be sober, watch. Tonight, before you sleep, give the day one honest look back, even thirty seconds, phone down. Day six hundred eleven.

screen: `DAY 611 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A THOUSAND YEARS AS A DAY.`

howItsDone: In the Liturgy of the Hours, Night Prayer (Compline) begins with an examination of conscience and, on Tuesdays, has 1 Peter 5:8–9 as its short reading; priests, religious and many lay Catholics pray it before sleep.

fork.reveal: Peter falls asleep, more than once. years later the same man writes to the whole Church: be sober and watch.

original.note: Latin: be sober, watch: the words that opened Compline in the older Roman breviary.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scary line about the devil.
what it means: stay clear-headed and awake, stand firm in faith, and remember the whole Church is in it with you.
what a scholar hears: watch is the verb Jesus used in Gethsemane when Peter slept; the Church set the verses at Compline, the prayer before sleep.

notes: Tuesday Night Prayer short reading 1 Peter 5:8–9a in the current Liturgy of the Hours; in the pre-1970 Roman Breviary the lectio brevis 'Fratres: Sobrii estote et vigilate…' opened Compline daily. Confirm both.
Latin 'sobrii estote, vigilate' from the Vulgate of 1 Peter 5:8. Confirm.
Grēgoreō (watch) is the verb in Mark 14:34–38 / Matthew 26:38–41. Peter falls asleep three times in Mark and Matthew. Confirm.
'Lions hunt at night and look for the one drifted from the herd' is a general nature picture, not a claim from the text. Confirm it's acceptable.
Devil as a fallen creature with limited power: CCC 391–395. Confirm.
